newsitem.title: USA: Some investors not ready for U.S. market downturn.
newsitem.headline: Some investors not ready for U.S. market downturn.

text.p: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt said Thursday he is concerned many investors are not prepared for a potential downturn in the U.S. stock market.
"I always worry in the face of an exuberant market about investors who are more emotional than intellectual about their investment decisions," Levitt told Reuters in an interview.
His fears come as Wall Street stocks have surged, with the Dow instrustrials reaching all-time highs and many market players bracing themselves for a correction.
"My experience in the markets tells me that markets don't go one way and investors have to be prepared for volatility, particularly in markets that have become as globalized as ours," he said.

But investors, Levitt cautioned, aren't the only ones that need to brace themselves for a market downturn. More improvement among regulators both at home and internationally is needed to handle potential market disasters, he said.
"There are vast holes of information gathering around the globe," Levitt warned. He said only a handful of countries have taken big steps to improve coordination.

Regulators across national borders, he said, must be able to monitor firms in other countries, especially with computerized trading systems and technology advances that have blurred national boundaries.
"We've done that by jointly inspecting leading institutions in each of our countries and sharing that information," Levitt said of an arrangement with the United Kingdom, Canada and Switzerland.
"Were we to extend that practice to other countries around the globe, I think we'd be in a better position to anticipate risk," he said.
In the United States, Levitt said regulators have heightened efforts to coordinate work in a market downturn, noting that the cooperation among U.S. regulators has worked "reasonably well."

"The various regulators have talked about what-if scenarios, and staffs are constantly working through risk management strategies," Levitt said. But he added that cooperation among U.S. regulators stands to be improved.
"I think it's pretty good; it's not perfect," he said.
